title: Blog 1
content:
DEPLOYING FROM GITHUB ACTIONS TO AWS WITHOUT ACCESS KEYS: HOW DOES OIDC WORK? Introduction NexusOMS uses GitHub Actions to deploy the backend to ECR/ECS and the frontend to S3/CloudFront. This article explains how OpenID Connect (OIDC) and AWS STS give workflow jobs temporary credentials instead of storing long-lived access keys in GitHub Secrets.
Key points Request a token: The workflow obtains a GitHub OIDC token identifying the job, with claims such as aud and sub. Assume the role: The workflow presents the token to AWS STS through AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Validate conditions: AWS checks the token and the IAM role trust policy. Conditions must restrict the repository, branch and audience using the repository’s actual OIDC configuration. Issue credentials: STS returns temporary credentials for the job to call AWS APIs when the checks succeed. Limit operations: The role’s permission policy defines deployment access to ECR, ECS, S3 and CloudFront. Lessons learned The trust policy determines which workflow may assume the role; the permission policy determines what the role may do. Both must be checked when a pipeline returns AccessDenied, rather than creating long-lived access keys or broadening permissions just to make it run.

title: Workshop overview
content:
NexusOMS uses CloudFront as the public entry point, S3 for the React frontend, and an ALB to route /api/* to ECS Fargate tasks in private subnets. Each task runs the API and background worker in the same .NET application. The API sends events to SQS FIFO; the worker polls, processes and deletes messages after success. Failed messages move to the dead-letter queue according to the redrive policy.
The built-in Webhook Simulator generates order creation, cancellation and burst scenarios. The demo verifies orders and stock inside NexusOMS; live shop APIs are not integrated. The Open API branch in the diagram represents planned integration.
Supabase provides both PostgreSQL and the authentication already integrated into the application. RDS PostgreSQL replaces only the database; replacing all of Supabase also requires a separate authentication solution.
GitHub Actions sends an OIDC token to AWS STS to assume the IAM role and receive temporary credentials. The workflow uses these credentials to push the backend image to ECR, update the ECS service, build the frontend, synchronize it to S3, and create a CloudFront invalidation.
Numbered architecture flow Flow Description 1 The user accesses the system through CloudFront. 2 CloudFront loads the React frontend from S3. 3 CloudFront forwards /api/* requests to the Application Load Balancer. 4 The ALB routes requests to healthy Fargate tasks. 5 The API sends valid webhook events to SQS FIFO. 6 The worker polls SQS, processes messages in message-group order and deletes them after success. 7 Failed messages that exceed the receive limit move to the dead-letter queue. 8 Fargate uses the NAT Gateway in its Availability Zone for outbound traffic. 9 The NAT Gateway routes outbound traffic through the Internet Gateway. 10 The backend connects to Supabase; marketplace Open API access is planned integration. 11 GitHub Actions builds and pushes the backend image to ECR. 12 GitHub Actions registers a new task definition revision and updates the ECS service. 13 ECS deploys the new revision as Fargate tasks according to the desired count. 14 At startup, Fargate downloads ECR image layers from AWS-managed S3 through the S3 Gateway Endpoint. 15 The ALB writes access logs to the S3 audit bucket. 16 CloudTrail writes management events to the S3 audit bucket. The unnumbered dashed line from GitHub Actions to AWS STS represents OIDC authentication to obtain temporary credentials for CI/CD.
Flows 5–6 apply to both API + Worker replicas in one ECS service. Flow 14 covers the complete Fargate → Endpoint → S3 route. ECR API/registry access still uses NAT Gateways.
To demonstrate both tasks shown in the diagram, set Desired tasks = 2 and confirm one running task in each AZ. The lab uses 1 task by default.
Deployment flow Prepare the repository, Supabase, and local environment. Create the VPC, subnets, routes, NAT gateways, and security groups. Create the secret, log group, IAM roles, SQS FIFO queue, DLQ, and audit logs. Deploy the backend with ECR, ALB, and ECS Fargate. Deploy the frontend with S3 and CloudFront. Connect GitHub Actions to AWS using OIDC. Verify orders, cancellation, and the SQS burst demonstration. Clean the demo data and delete all AWS resources.

title: Blog 2
content:
ECS FARGATE FAILS TO START: DISTINGUISHING TASK ROLE AND EXECUTION ROLE Introduction When the NexusOMS ASP.NET Core backend was deployed to ECS Fargate, the service existed but its tasks repeatedly stopped with ResourceInitializationError and AccessDenied for secretsmanager:GetSecretValue. This article uses that failure to distinguish the two IAM roles in a task definition.
Key points Execution role: ECS uses this role to pull images from ECR, send logs and retrieve secrets referenced by the task definition. Task role: Application code uses this role when calling AWS APIs at runtime, such as sending and receiving SQS messages. Identify the required permission: ECS retrieves the connection string from Secrets Manager before the container starts, so GetSecretValue belongs in the execution role. A customer managed KMS key also requires checking decrypt permissions. Read the error: Identify the denied identity, action, resource and time of the call. Grant access to the correct secret instead of attaching AdministratorAccess. Verify the result: Monitor the replacement task, Healthy targets and API responses. An HTTP 500 caused by an invalid connection string is investigated separately from IAM failures. Lessons learned An Active service does not prove that the application works. Before adding a policy, identify who calls AWS, which action is called, which resource is accessed and when the call occurs. This helps correct the right role without granting excessive permissions.
References IAM for Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate — Wilklins Nyatteng Amazon ECS task execution IAM role Published article and evidence The Vietnamese article was approved and published in AWS Study Group.

title: CloudWatch alarms
content:
Create these alarms after the ALB, target group, and SQS queues are running.
1. Get the ALB and target-group dimensions Open PowerShell:
$AwsProfile = "nexusoms-demo" $AwsRegion = "ap-southeast-1" $AlbArn = aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --profile $AwsProfile --region $AwsRegion --names nexusoms-demo-alb --query "LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn" --output text $TargetGroupArn = aws elbv2 describe-target-groups --profile $AwsProfile --region $AwsRegion --names nexusoms-demo-api-tg --query "TargetGroups[0].TargetGroupArn" --output text $AlbDimension = $AlbArn.Substring($AlbArn.IndexOf("loadbalancer/") + "loadbalancer/".Length) $TargetGroupDimension = $TargetGroupArn.Substring($TargetGroupArn.IndexOf("targetgroup/")) "ALB_DIMENSION=$AlbDimension" "TARGET_GROUP_DIMENSION=$TargetGroupDimension" 2. Create the unhealthy-target alarm aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --profile $AwsProfile --region $AwsRegion --alarm-name nexusoms-demo-alb-unhealthy-targets --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB --metric-name UnHealthyHostCount --dimensions "Name=LoadBalancer,Value=$AlbDimension" "Name=TargetGroup,Value=$TargetGroupDimension" --statistic Minimum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 2 --threshold 0 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching The alarm enters ALARM when the target is unhealthy for at least two of three one-minute periods.
3. Create the dead-letter queue alarm aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --profile $AwsProfile --region $AwsRegion --alarm-name nexusoms-demo-webhook-dlq-visible --namespace AWS/SQS --metric-name ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible --dimensions "Name=QueueName,Value=nexusoms-demo-webhook-dlq.fifo" --statistic Maximum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 2 --threshold 0 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching The alarm enters ALARM when the DLQ contains messages for at least two of three one-minute periods.
4. Verify aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --profile $AwsProfile --region $AwsRegion --alarm-names nexusoms-demo-alb-unhealthy-targets nexusoms-demo-webhook-dlq-visible --query "MetricAlarms[].{Name:AlarmName,State:StateValue,Metric:MetricName}" --output table Open CloudWatch → Alarms → All alarms and confirm that both alarms exist. The lab does not configure SNS, so alarm state is visible only in CloudWatch.

title: Build and push the backend image
content:
Open PowerShell in the repository root.
1. Log in to ECR and build the image $Region = "ap-southeast-1" $AccountId = aws sts get-caller-identity ` --profile nexusoms-demo ` --query Account ` --output text $EcrRepositoryUri = "$AccountId.dkr.ecr.$Region.amazonaws.com/nexusoms-demo-api" $Registry = $EcrRepositoryUri.Split('/')[0] $ImageTag = "v1-initial" aws ecr get-login-password --profile nexusoms-demo --region $Region | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $Registry docker build ` --file backend/Dockerfile ` --tag "nexusoms-demo-api:$ImageTag" ` backend The login result must be Login Succeeded, and the Docker build must complete.
2. Tag and push the image docker tag ` "nexusoms-demo-api:$ImageTag" ` "$EcrRepositoryUri`:$ImageTag" docker push "$EcrRepositoryUri`:$ImageTag" $BackendImageUri = "$EcrRepositoryUri`:$ImageTag" $BackendImageUri Record $BackendImageUri for the task definition.
3. Troubleshoot Docker credentials on Windows If docker login reports The stub received bad data or docker push reports no basic auth credentials, do not rebuild the image. Push with a temporary Docker config:
The auth value in the temporary file is Base64-encoded, not encrypted. The file is created outside the repository and removed in finally.
$DockerConfigDir = Join-Path $env:TEMP "nexusoms-docker-$([guid]::NewGuid())" try { New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $DockerConfigDir -Force | Out-Null $EcrPassword = aws ecr get-login-password --profile nexusoms-demo --region $Region $Auth = [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes("AWS:$EcrPassword")) @{ auths = @{ $Registry = @{ auth = $Auth } } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 4 | Set-Content -LiteralPath (Join-Path $DockerConfigDir "config.json") -Encoding utf8 docker --config $DockerConfigDir push "$EcrRepositoryUri`:$ImageTag" } finally { Remove-Item -LiteralPath $DockerConfigDir -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue } Open the ECR repository and verify that the v1-initial tag and image digest are present.

title: Proposal
content:
This section summarizes the NexusOMS workshop proposal and the AWS demonstration that the team plans to conduct.
NexusOMS - Multi-Channel Order and Inventory Operations Platform A Practical AWS Deployment for Reliable Order, Inventory and Profit Operations 1. Executive Summary NexusOMS is built for a single organization that sells through Shopee, TikTok Shop, Lazada and Website D2C. It centralizes products, warehouses, inventory, marketplace orders, SKU mappings and order profitability. The implemented MVP uses a React/Vite frontend, a .NET 10 Modular Monolith API and Supabase for PostgreSQL and authentication. Access is restricted to the admin, manager and warehouse roles.
The system focuses on operational safety rather than ordinary CRUD. It supports atomic stock reservation, idempotent requests, signed simulated webhooks, SQS FIFO processing, inventory transactions and CM1–CM3 profitability. Real marketplace accounts are not available, so the team uses a simulator with payload structures inspired by marketplace APIs to demonstrate the order lifecycle.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Multi-channel sellers frequently switch between marketplace dashboards to manage orders and stock. Concurrent flash-sale orders may oversell a SKU, repeated webhook delivery may create duplicate records, and profit is difficult to understand after product cost, payment fees, fulfillment cost and advertising.
The Solution NexusOMS receives a simulated marketplace webhook, verifies its HMAC signature, and places the valid event on an Amazon SQS FIFO queue. An ECS worker consumes the message, maps the channel SKU to an internal product, and reserves available inventory in a database transaction. The order can then move through confirmation, preparation, shipment, delivery, or cancellation. Cancelling before dispatch releases reserved stock. Idempotency keys and database constraints prevent duplicate delivery from generating a second business operation, while messages that repeatedly fail move to a dead-letter queue.
Benefits and Return on Investment The platform creates one operating view for products, stock and orders, reducing manual reconciliation between channels. Reservation and commit/release operations make flash-sale behavior demonstrable and auditable. This workshop validates the technical solution and does not calculate financial ROI without measured operating data.
3. Solution Architecture The current application runs locally with React/Vite, a .NET 10 API and Supabase Cloud. The target demonstration architecture serves the frontend from Amazon S3 through CloudFront, sends API requests through an Application Load Balancer, and runs the API as an Amazon ECS Fargate service in two private subnets across two Availability Zones. Amazon SQS FIFO decouples webhook intake from business processing, and a dead-letter queue isolates messages that repeatedly fail. Each Availability Zone uses its own NAT Gateway so outbound connectivity remains available if one AZ fails. AWS WAF protects the application from common malicious requests. The workshop uses the default CloudFront domain and certificate, so it does not create AWS Certificate Manager resources. CloudTrail and ALB access logs are stored in one private S3 audit bucket.
Numbered Architecture Flow No. Flow 1 The user accesses the system through CloudFront. 2 CloudFront loads the React frontend from S3. 3 CloudFront forwards /api/* requests to the Application Load Balancer. 4 The ALB routes requests to healthy Fargate tasks. 5 The API validates a webhook and sends the message to SQS FIFO. 6 The background worker in Fargate polls SQS, processes messages in message-group order and deletes them after successful processing. 7 Messages that exceed the receive limit move to the dead-letter queue. 8 Fargate uses the NAT Gateway in its Availability Zone for outbound traffic. 9 The NAT Gateway routes outbound traffic through the Internet Gateway. 10 The backend connects to Supabase; the sales-platform Open API branch represents planned integration that is not implemented in the demo. 11 GitHub Actions builds and pushes the backend image to ECR. 12 GitHub Actions registers the task definition and updates the ECS service. 13 ECS deploys the new image as Fargate tasks in two Availability Zones. 14 At task startup, Fargate downloads ECR image layers from AWS-managed S3 through the S3 Gateway Endpoint. Number 14 covers the entire Fargate → Endpoint → S3 route. 15 The ALB writes access logs to the S3 audit bucket. 16 CloudTrail writes management events to the S3 audit bucket. The unnumbered dashed line from GitHub Actions to AWS STS represents CI/CD OIDC authentication rather than a business flow.
The two Fargate tasks are replicas of the same application in one ECS service. Each task runs the API and background worker in the same .NET process. Flows 5–6 apply to both replicas, not communication between tasks or separate services. To demonstrate the two-AZ configuration, set Desired tasks = 2 and confirm one running task in each AZ; the lab uses one task by default.
The sales-platform Open API block represents planned integration. The demo uses the built-in Webhook Simulator to generate order creation, cancellation and burst events on demand. Order and stock changes are verified inside NexusOMS; they are not synchronized with live shops. Outbound flow 10 does not represent incoming marketplace webhooks.
AWS Services Used Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudFront: Store and distribute the static React/Vite build. AWS WAF: Protects the application from common malicious requests. Application Load Balancer: Routes API traffic to healthy ECS tasks. Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate: Runs the containerized .NET 10 API across two Availability Zones. Amazon ECR: Stores versioned backend container images built from GitHub CI. AWS STS: Validates the GitHub OIDC token and issues temporary credentials to GitHub Actions. Amazon SQS FIFO and a dead-letter queue: Buffer webhook bursts, preserve ordering within a message group, and isolate failed messages. Amazon VPC, NAT Gateway and Internet Gateway: Isolate API tasks in private subnets while allowing controlled outbound access. S3 Gateway Endpoint: Downloads image layers from the AWS-managed S3 storage used by ECR. This is separate from the frontend and audit buckets. The backend does not currently store product images, invoices or reports in S3. AWS Secrets Manager and Amazon CloudWatch: Manage application configuration and collect logs/metrics. ECR API/registry, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch Logs and SQS use NAT Gateways in the lab; S3 traffic uses the Gateway Endpoint. AWS CloudTrail and Amazon S3: Record management events and retain CloudTrail/ALB access logs in a private audit bucket. Supabase Cloud: Provides both PostgreSQL and the Supabase Auth integration already used by the application. Keeping Supabase lets the lab focus on AWS deployment. RDS PostgreSQL can replace the database, but replacing all of Supabase also requires a separate authentication solution. Component Design Frontend: React/Vite presents product, warehouse, order, profit and webhook-simulation workflows. API: .NET 10 Modular Monolith exposes REST endpoints, validates Supabase JWTs and applies role policies. Order and inventory workflow: PostgreSQL transactions reserve, release or commit stock while preserving an inventory-operation record. Asynchronous webhook workflow: The API receives simulator payloads and sends them to SQS FIFO. The external webhook endpoint checks HMAC signatures; the simulator UI requires Manager/Admin access. A background worker in the same application polls the queue, processes messages and deletes them after success. The DLQ isolates failures according to the redrive policy. Order cancellation workflow: An order.cancelled event records the reason, changes the order state, and releases reserved inventory when the order has not been dispatched. Idempotency prevents stock from being released twice. Database and identity: Supabase provides PostgreSQL and Auth; the database uses a single-organization public schema. AWS runtime: The execution role lets ECS retrieve images, send logs and read secrets referenced by the task definition. The task role grants SQS access to application code. The backend reaches Supabase through NAT Gateways; the simulator runs inside the application. CI/CD: GitHub Actions uses OIDC to call AWS STS, receives temporary credentials, pushes images to ECR, updates the ECS service, syncs the frontend to S3, and creates a CloudFront invalidation. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts-completing the NexusOMS MVP and preparing a short AWS demonstration-each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: review the order/inventory domain, inspect the existing codebase and draw the target AWS architecture. Calculate Price and Check Practicality: use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate the selected-region, short-duration demonstration cost and adjust if needed. Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: review security groups, IAM permissions, NAT usage, image delivery and cleanup scope before deployment. Develop, Test, and Deploy: test frontend/backend flows locally, build the API container, deploy the selected AWS services, verify logs and remove temporary resources after the demonstration. Technical Requirements
NexusOMS Application: React/Vite frontend, .NET 10 API, PostgreSQL/Npgsql, Supabase Auth JWT verification, role policies and HMAC webhook validation. AWS Demonstration: Docker image in ECR, ECS Fargate service behind ALB, SQS FIFO plus a DLQ for webhooks, S3/CloudFront frontend, two public plus two private subnets, NAT Gateways, CloudWatch logs, Secrets Manager and AWS IAM roles. Supabase environment values are stored as secrets, not committed to source control. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Preparation: finalize source-code flows, test cases, architecture diagram and AWS cost worksheet. Demonstration setup: Configure the network, IAM roles, ECR, S3/CloudFront and observability resources. Deploy the container service and configure ALB, CloudFront, audit logs and secrets. Run webhook, order, inventory, and SQS burst demonstrations; inspect the DLQ, clean up DEMO-* records, and capture report evidence. Post-Demonstration: delete temporary AWS resources and retain only code, diagrams, screenshots and cost evidence for the report. 6. Budget Estimation The estimate was prepared in AWS Pricing Calculator for Asia Pacific (Singapore) / ap-southeast-1. The values below are the costs for one month of the demo configuration and usage entered in the Calculator. The actual bill may differ based on traffic, Free Tier eligibility and taxes.
Infrastructure Costs Service Estimate (USD/month) Amazon ECS Fargate 3.75 Application Load Balancer 18.98 2 NAT Gateways 86.14 Amazon S3 0.02 Amazon ECR 0.20 Amazon CloudWatch 0.07 AWS Secrets Manager 0.13 Amazon CloudTrail 0.00 Amazon CloudFront 0.00 Amazon SQS FIFO and Dead-letter Queue 0.05 AWS WAF 14.00 Total monthly cost 123.34 The SQS estimate assumes 100,000 billable FIFO requests per month at $0.50 per million requests, without applying Free Tier. The Calculator reports $0.00 upfront cost. The full configuration with two NAT Gateways and AWS WAF is estimated at $123.34 per month, before tax.
Cost-saving option A learning environment can use one NAT Gateway and omit AWS WAF. NAT Gateway cost then decreases to approximately $43.07 per month, reducing the total estimate to $66.27 per month and saving approximately $57.07 per month. This option accepts the NAT Gateway as a single point of failure and removes the application-protection layer provided by AWS WAF.
The workshop creates two CloudWatch metric alarms for unhealthy ALB targets and the SQS dead-letter queue. Monitoring cost remains grouped under Amazon CloudWatch instead of adding another service row. Keep the approved estimate and compare it with AWS Billing after the demo. The lab does not attach an SNS notification.
Hardware: No additional hardware is required; the project uses the existing development machines and Supabase Cloud project. 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Marketplace credentials unavailable: Medium impact, high probability. Stock conflict or duplicate webhook: High impact, medium probability. AWS cost overrun during the demonstration: Medium impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Marketplace integration: use the HMAC-protected simulator and documented representative payloads. Order/inventory integrity: use SQS FIFO, a DLQ, idempotency keys, database constraints and reserve/release/commit transactions. Cost: create AWS Budgets/billing alerts, constrain the demo duration and delete chargeable resources afterwards. Contingency Plans Run the complete functional demonstration locally with Supabase if an AWS deployment service is unavailable. Keep infrastructure definitions and the architecture diagram so the demonstration environment can be recreated and removed predictably. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: One system demonstrates product/SKU mapping, warehouse inventory, an order lifecycle including cancellation, asynchronous webhook safety and profitability instead of isolated manual workflows.
Long-term Value The MVP and AWS architecture form a reusable foundation for real marketplace credentials, production webhook adapters and future reporting improvements.

title: Blog 3
content:
DEPLOYING A .NET REST API ON ECS FARGATE: FROM DOCKER IMAGE TO RUNNING CONTAINER Introduction For NexusOMS, the team packages the .NET REST API as a Docker image and deploys it on Amazon ECS Fargate. The article follows the image build through to serving requests, with ECS orchestrating tasks and Fargate providing compute without requiring the team to manage EC2 servers.
Key points Build and push the image: GitHub Actions builds the backend, tags the image by version and pushes it to Amazon ECR. Task Definition: The pipeline registers a new revision describing the image, CPU, memory, ports, environment variables, secrets, logging and IAM roles. ECS Service: The service updates its revision and maintains the desired task count. The two-AZ architecture uses two tasks, one per AZ; the lab defaults to one task. Networking and health checks: The ALB uses two public subnets. Fargate runs in private subnets with awsvpc, a network interface per task and an ip target group. The ALB checks health before routing traffic to a new task. Permissions and configuration: The execution role supports image pulls, secret retrieval and logging; the task role grants SQS access to code. Secrets Manager supplies the connection string and webhook signing secret at startup. Lessons learned Pushing an image does not prove the API works. Verify the Task Definition revision, RUNNING tasks, Healthy targets and API responses; use CloudWatch Logs to investigate failures. With the circuit breaker and rollback enabled, ECS can restore the previous successful deployment if the new deployment fails.

title: GitHub Actions CI/CD
content:
Run this section only after the manual deployment is healthy.
1. Add the GitHub OIDC provider IAM → Identity providers → Add provider:
Provider type: OpenID Connect Provider URL: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com Audience: sts.amazonaws.com AWS STS validates the OIDC token against the IAM role trust policy. When aud and sub match, STS returns temporary credentials to the workflow. Do not create a separate STS resource.
2. Create the GitHub Actions role IAM → Roles → Create role → Web identity:
Identity provider: token.actions.githubusercontent.com Audience: sts.amazonaws.com GitHub organization: <GITHUB_OWNER> GitHub repository: <GITHUB_REPOSITORY> GitHub branch: main Role name: nexusoms-demo-github-actions-role gh auth status $GitHubOwner = "<GITHUB_OWNER>" $GitHubRepository = "nexus-aws" $ViewerPermission = gh repo view "$GitHubOwner/$GitHubRepository" --json viewerPermission --jq .viewerPermission if ($ViewerPermission -ne "ADMIN") { throw "The fork must return viewerPermission=ADMIN" } $OidcCustomization = gh api "repos/$GitHubOwner/$GitHubRepository/actions/oidc/customization/sub" | ConvertFrom-Json $OidcCustomization | ConvertTo-Json if ($OidcCustomization.use_immutable_subject -and $OidcCustomization.sub_claim_prefix) { $OidcSubject = "$($OidcCustomization.sub_claim_prefix):ref:refs/heads/main" } else { $OidcSubject = "repo:${GitHubOwner}/${GitHubRepository}:ref:refs/heads/main" } "VIEWER_PERMISSION=$ViewerPermission" "OIDC_SUBJECT=$OidcSubject" Copy the exact OIDC_SUBJECT value into the trust policy. If the workflow later uses a GitHub Environment, read the OIDC configuration again and replace the sub condition with the environment subject.
If gh auth status shows that you are signed out, run gh auth login first.
After creating nexusoms-demo-github-actions-role, open Trust relationships → Edit trust policy. Replace <ACCOUNT_ID> and <OIDC_SUBJECT>, then paste the complete policy:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com", "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "<OIDC_SUBJECT>" } } } ] } Choose Update policy. title: Secrets Manager
content:
Store all four values in one JSON secret. Do not create four separate secrets.
1. Prepare the Values JSON key Required value postgresConnectionString Npgsql Session pooler string with the database password supabaseUrl Project URL, not a database connection string systemActorId UUID of the active demo profile webhookSigningSecret Random string with at least 32 characters webhookSigningSecret verifies HMAC signatures at the simulated webhook endpoint; it is an application secret, not an AWS secret access key. ECS retrieves configuration through the execution role, while backend code accesses SQS through the task role.
Get these values from Supabase:
Session pooler: choose Connect → Session pooler, then copy the host, port, and username. Database password: use the Supabase database password. Project URL: open Project Settings → API → Project URL. Profile UUID: open SQL Editor → New query and run: select id, email from public.profiles where lower(email) = lower('<LOGIN_EMAIL>') limit 1; Copy the UUID of the demo account. Do not generate a random UUID.
2. Create the Secret Open AWS Secrets Manager → Store a new secret.
Select:
Secret type: Other type of secret Open the Plaintext tab. Replace every placeholder and paste the complete JSON block:
{ "postgresConnectionString": "Host=<SESSION_POOLER_HOST>;Port=5432;Database=postgres;Username=<POOLER_USERNAME>;Password=<DATABASE_PASSWORD>;SSL Mode=Require;Trust Server Certificate=true", "supabaseUrl": "https://<PROJECT_REF>.supabase.co", "systemActorId": "<PROFILE_UUID>", "webhookSigningSecret": "<RANDOM_SECRET_AT_LEAST_32_CHARACTERS>" } Choose Next and enter:
Secret name: nexusoms/demo/application Choose Next → Next → Store.
3. Copy the Secret ARN Open the new secret and copy the complete Secret ARN.
Save the ARN for the nexusoms-demo-ecs-execution-role policy in the next step.
4. Verify Open Secret value → Retrieve secret value and confirm these four keys exist:
postgresConnectionString supabaseUrl systemActorId webhookSigningSecret Validate the connection string format without printing the password:
$AwsProfile = "nexusoms-demo" $AwsRegion = "ap-southeast-1" $SecretId = "nexusoms/demo/application" $Secret = aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --profile $AwsProfile --region $AwsRegion --secret-id $SecretId --query SecretString --output text | ConvertFrom-Json $Builder = [System.Data.Common.DbConnectionStringBuilder]::new() $ParsedActorId = [guid]::Empty try { $Builder.set_ConnectionString([string]$Secret.postgresConnectionString) "postgresConnectionString: valid" } catch { "postgresConnectionString: invalid" } "supabaseUrl: $([uri]::IsWellFormedUriString([string]$Secret.supabaseUrl, [System.UriKind]::Absolute))" "systemActorId: $([guid]::TryParse([string]$Secret.systemActorId, [ref]$ParsedActorId))" "webhookSigningSecret: $(([string]$Secret.webhookSigningSecret).Length -ge 32)" Continue only when all four checks are valid.
These checks validate the JSON structure, URL, UUID, and connection-string syntax only. A 200 response from /health and a Healthy target confirm that the application responds; they do not test database connectivity.

title: ECS IAM roles
content:
Create an execution role for ECS and a task role for the application.
Step 1: Create the execution role Open IAM → Roles → Create role.
Trusted entity type: AWS service Service or use case: Elastic Container Service Task Attach:
AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy Enter the role name and create the role:
nexusoms-demo-ecs-execution-role Step 2: Allow the execution role to read the secret Open the new role → Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON.
Replace <SECRET_ARN> with the complete secret ARN:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ReadNexusOmsApplicationSecret", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue", "Resource": "<SECRET_ARN>" } ] } Save the policy as:
ReadNexusOmsApplicationSecret Use the secret ARN in Resource. Add the :jsonKey:: suffix only in the Task Definition ValueFrom field.
Step 3: Create the task role Create a second role with the same trusted entity:
nexusoms-demo-ecs-task-role Do not attach AdministratorAccess. Add the SQS permissions after creating the queues.
Step 4: Verify the roles $AwsProfile = "nexusoms-demo" $AwsRegion = "ap-southeast-1" $SecretArn = aws secretsmanager describe-secret --profile $AwsProfile --region $AwsRegion --secret-id nexusoms/demo/application --query ARN --output text aws iam list-attached-role-policies --profile $AwsProfile --role-name nexusoms-demo-ecs-execution-role aws iam list-role-policies --profile $AwsProfile --role-name nexusoms-demo-ecs-execution-role aws iam get-role-policy --profile $AwsProfile --role-name nexusoms-demo-ecs-execution-role --policy-name ReadNexusOmsApplicationSecret --query "PolicyDocument.Statement[?Action=='secretsmanager:GetSecretValue'].Resource" --output text $SecretArn aws iam get-role --profile $AwsProfile --role-name nexusoms-demo-ecs-task-role --query "Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument.Statement[].Principal.Service" --output text Expected result:
The execution role has AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy and ReadNexusOmsApplicationSecret. The ARN returned by get-role-policy matches $SecretArn. The IAM resource ARN does not include :jsonKey::. The task role trusts ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com. After changing the policy, run Force new deployment and inspect the new task. The stopped reason of an older task does not reflect the updated policy.

title: CloudFront Function for SPA
content:
Create a CloudFront Function that serves React routes without file extensions from /index.html.
Step 1: Create the function Open CloudFront → Functions → Create function.
Function name: nexusoms-demo-spa-routing Runtime: cloudfront-js-2.0 Step 2: Open Build and add the SPA rewrite code Open the function, choose the Build tab, delete the sample code, and paste this entire block:
function handler(event) { var request = event.request; var uri = request.uri; // Rewrite SPA routes to index.html while preserving static files. if (uri === "/" || uri.indexOf(".") === -1) { request.uri = "/index.html"; } return request; } Step 3: Build and publish the function Follow this order:
Choose Save changes in the Build tab. Choose Publish. Confirm that the function is in the LIVE stage. If Create or Publish reports UnknownError, refresh the Functions list and check whether the function was created or published before retrying.
Step 4: Associate the function with the distribution Open the distribution → Behaviors → select Default (*) → Edit.
Under Function associations, select:
Event type: Viewer request Function type: CloudFront Functions Function ARN/Name: nexusoms-demo-spa-routing Stage: LIVE Do not associate the function with the /api/* behavior.
Do not configure distribution-wide custom 403/404 responses that return /index.html with HTTP 200. The function rewrites only frontend routes on the Default behavior, while API errors keep their original status and body.
Step 5: Verify the association Confirm that the function is LIVE and associated with Viewer request on Default (*), then wait for the distribution to become Deployed. Copy its domain name for Build and upload the frontend.
After uploading the frontend and completing the invalidation, open /app?page=dashboard to verify SPA routing.

title: SQS FIFO and Dead-letter Queue
content:
Create the dead-letter queue first. Then create the webhook queue and attach the redrive policy.
The API sends simulated order creation/cancellation events to the queue (flow 5). A background worker in the same application polls, processes and deletes messages after success (flow 6). Both Fargate tasks use the same queue; the lab does not require a separate worker service.
1. Create the Dead-letter Queue Open Amazon SQS → Create queue.
Use these values:
Type: FIFO Name: nexusoms-demo-webhook-dlq.fifo Visibility timeout: 60 seconds Message retention period: 4 days Content-based deduplication: Disabled Encryption: Amazon SQS managed key Access policy: Basic Dead-letter queue: Disabled Choose Create queue.
2. Create the Webhook Queue Choose Create queue and use these values:
Type: FIFO Name: nexusoms-demo-webhook-queue.fifo Visibility timeout: 60 seconds Message retention period: 1 day Delivery delay: 0 seconds Receive message wait time: 20 seconds Content-based deduplication: Disabled High throughput FIFO: Disabled Encryption: Amazon SQS managed key Access policy: Basic Dead-letter queue: nexusoms-demo-webhook-dlq.fifo Maximum receives: 3 Choose Create queue.
3. Get the Queue URLs and ARNs Run the complete PowerShell block:
$AwsRegion = "ap-southeast-1" $AwsProfile = "nexusoms-demo" $WebhookQueueName = "nexusoms-demo-webhook-queue.fifo" $WebhookDlqName = "nexusoms-demo-webhook-dlq.fifo" $WebhookQueueUrl = aws sqs get-queue-url ` --profile $AwsProfile ` --region $AwsRegion ` --queue-name $WebhookQueueName ` --query QueueUrl ` --output text $WebhookDlqUrl = aws sqs get-queue-url ` --profile $AwsProfile ` --region $AwsRegion ` --queue-name $WebhookDlqName ` --query QueueUrl ` --output text $WebhookQueueArn = aws sqs get-queue-attributes ` --profile $AwsProfile ` --region $AwsRegion ` --queue-url $WebhookQueueUrl ` --attribute-names QueueArn ` --query "Attributes.QueueArn" ` --output text $WebhookDlqArn = aws sqs get-queue-attributes ` --profile $AwsProfile ` --region $AwsRegion ` --queue-url $WebhookDlqUrl ` --attribute-names QueueArn ` --query "Attributes.QueueArn" ` --output text "WEBHOOK_QUEUE_URL=$WebhookQueueUrl" "WEBHOOK_QUEUE_ARN=$WebhookQueueArn" "WEBHOOK_DLQ_URL=$WebhookDlqUrl" "WEBHOOK_DLQ_ARN=$WebhookDlqArn" Save both Queue URLs for the ECS task definition.
4. Grant Access to the ECS Task Role Open IAM → Roles → nexusoms-demo-ecs-task-role.
Choose Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON.
Replace <ACCOUNT_ID> and paste this policy:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "UseWebhookQueue", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["sqs:SendMessage", "sqs:ReceiveMessage", "sqs:DeleteMessage", "sqs:GetQueueAttributes"], "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:ap-southeast-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:nexusoms-demo-webhook-queue.fifo" }, { "Sid": "ReadWebhookDeadLetterQueue", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sqs:GetQueueAttributes", "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:ap-southeast-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:nexusoms-demo-webhook-dlq.fifo" } ] } Save it as UseNexusOmsWebhookQueues. Attach it to the task role, not the execution role.
5. Verify Main queue: nexusoms-demo-webhook-queue.fifo DLQ: nexusoms-demo-webhook-dlq.fifo Maximum receives: 3 Task role policy: UseNexusOmsWebhookQueues

title: Build and upload the frontend
content:
Complete CloudFront distribution and CloudFront Function before building. Use the domain and Distribution ID you just created.
Open PowerShell in the repository root.
Keep the two CloudFront values separate:
Value Example Used for Domain d....cloudfront.net VITE_API_BASE_URL Distribution ID E... Invalidation command Verify that Git ignores the local production file:
git check-ignore frontend/.env.production.local 1. Build the frontend $CloudFrontDomain = "<CLOUDFRONT_DOMAIN>" $ProjectRef = "<PROJECT_REF>" $SupabaseAnonKey = "<SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_OR_ANON_KEY>" Push-Location frontend $env:VITE_DATA_MODE = "supabase" $env:VITE_API_BASE_URL = "https://$CloudFrontDomain" $env:VITE_SUPABASE_URL = "https://$ProjectRef.supabase.co" $env:VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY = $SupabaseAnonKey npm ci npm run typecheck npm run test npm run build Use only the Supabase publishable/anon key in a VITE_ variable. Do not use a service-role or secret key.
2. Upload to S3 $AccountId = aws sts get-caller-identity ` --profile nexusoms-demo ` --query Account ` --output text $BucketName = "nexusoms-demo-frontend-$AccountId" aws s3 sync .\dist "s3://$BucketName" ` --delete ` --profile nexusoms-demo ` --region ap-southeast-1 3. Create a CloudFront invalidation $DistributionId = "<CLOUDFRONT_DISTRIBUTION_ID>" $InvalidationId = aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id $DistributionId --paths "/*" --profile nexusoms-demo --query "Invalidation.Id" --output text aws cloudfront wait invalidation-completed --distribution-id $DistributionId --id $InvalidationId --profile nexusoms-demo Pop-Location Continue only after the wait command completes successfully.
4. Verify the website Open https://<CLOUDFRONT_DOMAIN>/app?page=dashboard and sign in with the demo account. Refresh the page to verify SPA routing.
Open the order list. In DevTools → Network, confirm that /api/v1/orders returns 200 with JSON data from the backend.
